steps.body: A fraction only has a name when the pieces are EQUAL. Three unequal scraps are not thirds — they are just three pieces.
steps.narration: A fraction only has a name when the pieces are EQUAL. Three unequal scraps are not thirds — they are just three pieces.

widget.prompt: Build a bar cut into 4 equal pieces with 1 shaded: make 1/4.
widget.successFeedback: 1/4 — four equal pieces, one of them shaded. Equal pieces are what earn the name.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

commonFractions.feedback: That is 1/3 — three equal pieces, not four. The denominator counts the pieces the whole became.
2/4 shades two of the four pieces; a unit fraction shades exactly one.

predict.prompt: A circle is cut into 3 pieces of different sizes. Are these thirds?
predict.reveal: Thirds means three EQUAL parts. Counting to three is not enough; the pieces must match.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f equal parts really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f equal parts comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: A circle is cut into 3 pieces, but one piece is much larger than the others. Are these thirds?

options.label: No — thirds must be three EQUAL pieces
options.feedback: Correct — a fraction name promises equal shares; three unequal pieces have no fraction name at all.

options.label: Yes — there are 3 pieces
options.feedback: Counting three pieces is not enough; the pieces must also be the same size to earn the name thirds.

options.label: Yes, if you agree to call them thirds
options.feedback: Naming does not make shares fair — the pieces themselves must match in size.

options.label: Only the biggest piece is a third
options.feedback: Picking the largest piece assumes size alone earns the name, but a third must be one of three MATCHING parts — and none of these match.

widget.prompt: A circle is split into thirds. How many equal pieces are there?

commonErrors.feedback: One is the whole, not the number of pieces — thirds names how many equal parts the whole becomes.
Two equal parts are halves. Thirds cut the same whole into one more piece.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the equal pieces the whole was cut into, then count how many of them the question is about.
